title: The Age of the Martyrs
subtitle: From Nero's fire to Diocletian's last storm. What Rome actually demanded, why believers died rather than comply, and what the church learned about mercy from the people who failed.

sections.title: What Rome Actually Wanted
sections.body:
Start by clearing away the movie version. Rome did not hunt Christians without pause for two and a half centuries, with legions combing the provinces for believers. For most of those years the persecution was local, occasional, and almost casual, a matter of mobs and governors rather than settled imperial policy. Around AD 112 a governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan asking what he was supposed to do with these people, admitting he had never attended a trial of Christians. Trajan's answer set the pattern for a century. Do not seek them out. Ignore anonymous accusations. But if someone is accused and will not recant, punish him. The church lived inside that answer for generations, legal enough to grow and illegal enough to die.

What Rome wanted was not agreement but a gesture. A pinch of incense on the altar, a word calling Caesar lord, and the accused walked free. The empire was broad-minded about gods, collecting them the way it collected provinces. What it could not tolerate was refusal, and the Christians refused. They would worship Jesus and no one else, and to Roman ears that obstinacy sounded like treason, and their private meetings sounded like conspiracy. The historian Tacitus, who despised them, records that Nero's victims in AD 64 were convicted of hatred of the human race. That was the actual charge, and it tells us more than any legend does. The quarrel was never about whether Jesus could be worshiped. Rome had room for one more god. It was about whether anything else must be.

sections.title: The People Who Would Not Say the Word
sections.body:
The deaths are recorded, and the records repay slow reading, because they are not legends. Around 165 the philosopher Justin, who had walked through every school in the ancient world before finding Christ, was beheaded in Rome with six companions after a trial whose record survives. Asked to sacrifice, he answered that no right-thinking person deserts truth for falsehood. In 177 mob violence in the Gallic city of Lyons swept up dozens of believers, and the survivors wrote a letter describing what followed. The one the crowds could not break was Blandina, a slave girl her friends had feared was too frail to hold out. She outlasted every torture applied to her and died still confessing, and the watchers admitted they had never seen a woman endure so much.

In 203 in Carthage, a twenty-two-year-old mother named Perpetua was arrested with a pregnant slave named Felicity. Perpetua kept a diary in prison, one of the earliest surviving Christian writings from a woman's hand. In it her father begs her, weeping, to think of her nursing son and say the word that would free her. She points to a water jug and asks whether it can be called anything other than what it is. Neither, she says, can she call herself anything but what she is, a Christian. She and Felicity died together in the arena, and the account of their deaths was read in churches for centuries.

Notice who these people were. A philosopher, a slave, a young mother. The sword fell across every rank of that society, and every rank produced someone who would not say the word.

sections.title: When the Empire Turned Its Whole Weight
sections.body:
For nearly two centuries the danger stayed local. Then the empire itself began to shake, with invasion on the frontiers and plague and inflation inside them, and emperors casting about for a cause found one in the people who would not sacrifice to the gods. In 250 the emperor Decius ordered every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice publicly and carry a certificate proving it. It was the first universal persecution, and it broke over a church grown comfortable in a long peace. Many believers died. Many more complied, or bought forged certificates from obliging officials, and the church would spend a generation deciding what to do about them.

Valerian struck next, in 257 and 258, aiming at bishops, clergy, and church property. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, was beheaded in 258 and met the sentence with the words thanks be to God. Then came four decades of calm, and then the worst of all. In 303 the emperor Diocletian, pressed hard by his junior colleague Galerius, ordered churches demolished, Scriptures burned, clergy imprisoned, and at last everyone made to sacrifice. The Great Persecution burned hottest in the east, where it killed and maimed for the better part of a decade. In 311 a dying Galerius, whose persecution had failed either to break the church or to appease his gods, issued an edict of grudging toleration and asked the Christians to pray for him. Two years later Constantine made the faith legal. The age of the martyrs ended not because Rome relented into kindness, but because Rome gave up.

sections.title: What to Do with the Ones Who Failed
sections.body:
Here is the part of the story the stained glass leaves out. Most Christians were not heroes. Under Decius the compliance was so widespread that in some cities the assemblies were nearly emptied, and when the storm passed, the lapsed came back, ashamed, asking to return. The church split over what to do with them. One party, led in Rome by a priest named Novatian, held that those who had denied Christ could never be restored by the church at all. Their case was serious, and it deserves stating honestly. The martyrs had died rather than say the word. To readmit the people who said it, the rigorists argued, was to announce to the next generation that the confession did not finally matter.

Cyprian and the larger church answered with a different severity, slower and harder. The lapsed could return, but through real repentance carried over time, weighed case by case, not waved through on a martyr's popularity. In choosing that path the church defined something permanent about the gospel. The body of Christ is not a hall of the undefeated. It is a company of the forgiven, or it is nothing, because its own Lord was abandoned by every man he had trained, and he fed them breakfast on a beach afterward.

The same fight returned after Diocletian, harder and longer, in the Donatist quarrel over clergy who had handed the Scriptures over to the authorities. The church never found a painless answer. It only kept refusing the clean one.

sections.title: Why They Grew Under the Sword
sections.body:
Around the year 197 the North African writer Tertullian threw a taunt at the persecutors that became the era's epitaph. Kill us, he wrote in effect, and we multiply, for the blood of Christians is seed. It was true, and it should be told carefully, because executions alone argued no one into faith. The historians point to quieter causes running underneath. Christians stayed in the plague cities and nursed the dying, including the pagan dying, when others fled. They took in the infants Rome left exposed. They buried the poor with dignity. Their assemblies seated slave beside senator in a world where that happened almost nowhere else. A century and a half later the emperor Julian, trying to revive paganism, complained in a letter that the Galileans fed not only their own poor but everyone else's, while his own priests fed no one. The church's argument was its life, and Rome had no answer to it.

The church also refused to make dying a strategy. The same account that records Polycarp's martyrdom pauses over a man named Quintus, who volunteered for arrest, boasted of it, and then broke at the sight of the beasts and sacrificed. We do not praise those who hand themselves over, the writers concluded, because the gospel does not teach it. Courage was demanded when the hour came and forbidden as a performance before it came. That distinction, between bearing a cross and building yourself one, took a wisdom the church has not always kept since.

sections.title: The Weight the Martyrs Leave on Us
sections.body:
It would be comfortable to close with admiration, and admiration is owed. But the age of the martyrs leaves two weights, and honesty requires carrying both. The first falls on the church that came after, which is to say on us. Within a century of Diocletian's fires, Christians held the power of the empire, and Christians began to reach for the sword, against heretics, against pagans, eventually against each other. The people of the catacombs became the people of the courtroom. Whatever else that reversal was, it was a forgetting, and the church has repeated it in every age when power came back within reach, including ages recent enough to implicate the people writing and reading this essay.

The second weight is quieter. The martyrs were not extraordinary people, and the records go out of their way to show it. A slave girl. A nursing mother. An old bishop. A philosopher with a stubborn streak. What held them up was not iron in the blood but a settled conviction that Jesus was Lord and Caesar was not, held so deep that the body obeyed it when the moment came. Most of us have never been asked the question they were asked, and it is cheap to assume we would have answered well. The lapsed were us. The martyrs, by grace, might have been. The era does not ask for our admiration. It asks whom we worship, and it waits for the answer.

keyFigures.name: Justin Martyr
keyFigures.note: Philosopher convert beheaded at Rome around 165, whose trial record survives.

keyFigures.name: Blandina of Lyons
keyFigures.note: Slave girl whose endurance in the persecution at Lyons in 177 outlasted every torture.

keyFigures.name: Perpetua and Felicity
keyFigures.note: A young mother and a slave, martyred together at Carthage in 203. Perpetua's prison diary survives.

keyFigures.name: Cyprian of Carthage
keyFigures.note: Bishop beheaded under Valerian in 258, who guided the church through the fight over the lapsed.

keyFigures.name: Tertullian of Carthage
keyFigures.note: North African writer who told Rome that the blood of Christians is seed.

keyFigures.name: Novatian
keyFigures.note: Roman rigorist who held that the lapsed could never return, the position the church refused.
